Chapter 3: Turning the Zoo into a Hidden Refuge
As the occupation tightened its grip, the Żabiński family’s home changed in ways they never could’ve imagined. Their villa, once lively with the sounds of animals, was now a crossroads—a secret haven for people desperate for safety. You could almost hear the tension in every whispered conversation and hurried footstep echoing through those rooms.
Each day, the Żabińskis added new layers of caution to their routines. Imagine it—every knock at the door, every stranger passing by, could mean danger. But even with that risk hanging over them, they pressed on, guided by a sense of duty that was bigger than just protecting themselves.
Jan’s work gave him rare access to the Warsaw Ghetto. He saw the suffering there up close—and he couldn’t just stand by. He began smuggling people out, hiding them in the zoo’s empty cages and outbuildings. Meanwhile, Antonina took charge of the household, determined to create a feeling of normal life for everyone in hiding. She cooked meals, cared for the sick, and somehow managed to lift spirits, even when the threat of being discovered was always just around the corner.
The boundaries between family and guest started to blur. People who found shelter with the Żabińskis became part of the daily rhythm—helping with chores, and even tending to the animals that were left. Those animals, in their own way, offered comfort too. A little bit of joy in a world that felt so uncertain. And Antonina—she had an uncanny ability to sense when someone was scared or losing hope. Her empathy often made all the difference.
The risks? They were enormous. The Nazis had one punishment for helping Jews—death. The Żabińskis knew that a single misstep could cost them everything. So, they created routines to avoid suspicion—using coded words, signals, anything to stay one step ahead. Sometimes, Antonina would play the piano as a warning sign for those in hiding. Even their young son learned to keep secrets most adults would struggle with. The villa was always tense, but you could feel a quiet determination too. Every act of kindness was an act of resistance.
Over time, the Warsaw Zoo became part of something bigger—a network of safe houses and escape routes. Jan worked with the Polish underground, helping people escape, or giving them false papers. Word began to spread: the Żabiński villa was a place of refuge. Those who made it there often carried heartbreaking stories of loss and survival. The Żabińskis listened, comforted, and helped however they could. And you start to see—resistance isn’t just about fighting with weapons. Sometimes, it’s about refusing to turn away from someone in need.
The trauma of war touched everyone in that villa—humans and animals alike. Animals can sense their caretakers’ moods, and they mirrored the tension and fear that filled the house. Yet, even with danger everywhere, moments of connection and joy could still be found. Maybe a child would laugh at a monkey’s silly antics, or a guest would find comfort in the gentle presence of a dog. It’s these small, everyday moments that reminded them all—compassion and courage can survive even in the darkest times.
